title: US set to unveil new tariffs on India and 15 other economies over 'excess capacity'
dek: Findings of a US trade investigation opened in March are expected as soon as this week, reports say. India has said it will not sign its interim trade deal until Washington's new tariff structure is clear.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The United States is preparing to announce new tariffs on India and 15 other economies that it accuses of building up excess industrial capacity, with the findings of a trade investigation opened in March expected as soon as this week, according to reports. The rates have not been disclosed, and any new duties would come on top of tariffs India's exporters already pay.

The timing puts fresh pressure on New Delhi's interim trade deal with Washington. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said last week that the deal was "more or less finalised" but would not be signed until the US settled its new tariff structure, according to reports. The excess-capacity investigation is the biggest unknown in that structure.

## What happened

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) opened the investigations on 11 March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the law that lets Washington impose duties on countries whose trade practices it finds "unreasonable or discriminatory" and burdensome to US commerce. The 16 economies are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Cambodia, Bangladesh, Switzerland, Norway and Mexico.

The USTR's fact sheet said the investigations would examine practices that it says create "structural excess capacity and production" in manufacturing, including subsidies, wage suppression, the role of state-owned enterprises and barriers to market access. It said the USTR had asked each government, including India's, for consultations. The formal notice was published in the US Federal Register on 17 March, written comments closed in April and public hearings were held from 5 May.

Reports on Tuesday and Wednesday said the USTR, led by Jamieson Greer, could release its findings as soon as this week. Mr Greer has argued that subsidies and other government support have let foreign companies flood world markets with cheap goods at the expense of US producers, reports said. People familiar with the plans said it was unclear what rates would be charged or what exemptions would be granted, and the USTR and the White House did not respond to requests for comment, one report said.

One report said the new duties would cover most imports from the 16 economies but would probably exclude goods already covered by separate US tariffs, such as steel, aluminium and cars. It said rates would be graduated, with lower caps for the EU, Japan and South Korea and possibly higher rates for China, India and Vietnam. China is expected to face some of the highest rates, according to another report.

## Background

Washington's tariff regime has been rebuilt piece by piece this year. In February the US Supreme Court struck down the tariffs President Donald Trump had imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), according to reports. That ruling also upended the India-US trade framework agreed the same month, which had to go back to negotiators. Mr Agrawal said last week that the court's judgment had made the earlier US offer of an 18% tariff on Indian goods irrelevant, according to reports.

The administration has since turned to Section 301, which sets no ceiling on the rate of duty. A separate Section 301 investigation into forced labour in supply chains led to duties of 10% or 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners from 24 July, including all 16 economies in the excess-capacity case. India was among those assigned the 10% rate, according to an analysis of the USTR's July notice. Any excess-capacity duties would be stacked on top of those, reports said.

India has said it wants a tariff rate lower than those of competing exporters such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia, according to reports. All three are also among the 16 economies under investigation, so the relative rates matter as much as the absolute ones for India's labour-intensive exports such as garments. For eastern India, the comparison with Bangladesh, the world's second-largest garment exporter, is especially close: the two countries compete for the same US apparel orders.

## What they are saying

The Indian government has not publicly responded to the latest reports. Mr Agrawal said on 18 November that every part of the bilateral deal had been more or less settled and that negotiations would conclude soon, but that India would wait for the new US tariff architecture before signing, according to reports. He also linked the signing to the pending Section 301 investigations.

The USTR has said only that the investigations will determine whether the 16 economies' practices burden US commerce "and what action, if any" should follow. Both the forced-labour and excess-capacity duties are expected to face legal challenges in US courts that could delay them, according to reports.

## What happens next

If the USTR follows the pattern of the forced-labour case, the findings would come with a proposed list of duties and a period for public comment before the tariffs take effect. In that case, the findings and proposed action were published on 5 June and the duties applied from 24 July. Under the law, the USTR has until 11 March 2027 to make a determination in the excess-capacity investigations.

For India, the questions are what rate it is assigned, which products are exempted, and how its rate compares with Bangladesh's, Vietnam's and China's. The answers will decide whether the interim trade deal can be signed this winter.

## Timeline

- 11 March 2026: USTR opens Section 301 excess-capacity investigations into 16 economies, including India
- 17 March: formal notice published in the Federal Register
- 5 May onwards: public hearings
- 5 June: findings and proposed duties published in the separate forced-labour case
- 24 July: forced-labour duties of 10% or 12.5% take effect on goods from 60 trading partners
- 18 November: Commerce Secretary says the India-US deal will be signed only after the new US tariff structure is clear
- This week: excess-capacity findings expected, according to reports
- 11 March 2027: statutory deadline for a determination
